phrases.explanation:
These two words open an action rather than describe anything. Allah taught the Prophet Muhammad to place the mention of His names before everything he did, and made that a practice for the whole community, so speech, letters, requests and ordinary acts all begin with it. The sense is not "by Allah" but "I begin with the naming and mention of Allah before anything else", or "I read while naming Allah".

A difficulty the passage raises is that the letter b at the front of the word needs a verb to introduce it, and no verb is spoken. The answer is that the listener already knows what the speaker intends, so saying it would be needless. Someone asked what he ate that day can answer simply "Food", because the question supplied the rest. In the same way, reciting the formula and then beginning a chapter shows that the meaning is "I read in the name of Allah", and saying it while standing up shows "I stand in the name of Allah". Every action carries its own unspoken verb with it.

A second question is whether "the name" simply means God Himself. The passage answers no, with two arguments. Scholars agree that a person slaughtering an animal who says "by Allah" instead of "in the name of Allah" has not said what was prescribed, which would not follow if the two phrases meant the same thing. And if a name were the one named, it would make sense to say "I saw the name of Zayd" or "I ate the name of the food", which no Arab accepts. Grammatically, the noun for name stands in place of the verbal noun for naming, a substitution Arabic allows freely. A report from one of the companions agrees, glossing the words as: read with the mention of Allah, your Lord.

The name is explained through worship. One report gives it as the One whom everything worships and all creatures serve. The passage then asks whether the word has a verb it is built from, and answers that it was not heard directly from the Arabs but follows by reasoning, since they do say of a man who devotes himself to worship that he "ta'allaha", and nobody disputes that usage. On this basis God required worship from the servant, and the servant worshipped Him. "Allah" is therefore originally "al-ilah", the God, worn together in speech, and some early readers are reported to have pronounced the longer form.

The name also comes first for a reason. Arabic puts the name of whoever is being spoken about before his descriptions, so that the listener knows who is meant. There is a further propriety in the order. Some of God's names may not be given to any creature, such as Allah, al-Rahman and al-Khaliq, while others, such as al-Rahim, al-Sami and al-Basir, are permitted to people. The names that belong to Him alone are placed first, because divinity belongs to no one else, neither in the naming nor in the meaning.

Both names come from mercy, and the passage begins with how they are built. Al-Rahman follows a pattern Arabic uses for a settled state, the way "to be angry" yields "angry" and "to be drunk" yields "drunk". Al-Rahim follows the pattern reserved for praise and blame, which Arabic applies even where the verb would suggest a different shape, as with "knowing" and "able". Had each name simply followed its verb, both would have come out as the same word, "the merciful".

That raises an objection. If both names mean mercy, what does the repetition add? The answer is that each carries something the other does not. In Arabic the first pattern departs further from the base verb than the second, and where a name departs further in the way of praise, the one described by it is greater. So al-Rahman says more than al-Rahim. The early exegetes disagreed about how exactly to state the difference, and two reports are given, one traced to the Prophet and one from a companion. Both are judged sound, since they can be reconciled.

The reconciliation is that al-Rahman describes a mercy that is universal and reaches the whole of creation, while al-Rahim describes a mercy that is particular and reaches a portion of it. Applied to the two worlds, God is Rahman toward everyone in this life and the next, in the provision, the rain, the crops, sound bodies and minds, and blessings too many to count, which believers and disbelievers share alike. He is Rahim toward the believers specifically, in the help He gives them to obey Him here, and in the gardens He has reserved for them in the Hereafter.

One further point is that al-Rahman is a name no creature may take, and the passage recalls Musaylima, the liar who claimed it for himself in the Prophet's lifetime and was cut off for it. It is suggested that God reserved the two names together for Himself alone. A claim that the Arabs did not know the word at all is then rejected: the polytheists who asked what al-Rahman might be were denying a name they recognised, just as they recognised the Prophet and denied him, and pre-Islamic poetry uses the word.

The meaning given is thankfulness belonging purely to Allah, to the exclusion of everything else that is worshipped and of every creature He has made, on account of favors that cannot be counted. Praise and thanks are treated as close enough to stand in for each other, since Arabic accepts the phrase "praise belongs to Allah as thanks", which would be impossible if the two words meant unrelated things. The name Allah itself has already been explained at the opening phrase, and the passage does not repeat that explanation here.

The definite article does real work here. With it, the sentence says that all praises and perfect thanks belong to Allah. Without it, a speaker would be reporting only his own act of praising. For that reason the reciters and the scholars are agreed on reading the word in the nominative rather than the accusative, since the accusative would turn the verse into "I praise Allah with a praising", the report of one person's deed rather than a statement about praise itself.

An objection follows. Has Allah praised Himself and then taught people to repeat it, and if so why does the chapter go on to say "You alone we worship"? The answer is that all of it is the speech of Allah. He praised Himself with what He is worthy of, then taught that praise to His servants and made reciting it a duty and a test. The command "say" is understood without being spoken, which is ordinary in Arabic. A person seeing a traveler off says "accompanied and protected", leaving out the verb "go", because the situation supplies it. The same omission is at work in the opening of this chapter.

The passage explains this word by the range it has in Arabic. A lord is the master who is obeyed in his affairs, the man who sets a thing in order and keeps it in repair, and the owner of a thing. Poets supply the evidence for each sense. One line of pre-Islamic poetry speaks of the lord of Kinda and means its master, another describes a favor that a man tends so that it lasts, and a third line speaks of guardianship passing from one ruler to another, the plural being rubub with rabb as its singular. Every other use of the word comes back to one of these three senses.

So the Lord named here is the Master who has no equal and no likeness in His loftiness, the One who orders the affairs of His creatures by the favors He has poured out on them, and the Owner to whom creation and command belong.

The worlds are the plural of a collective noun that has no singular of its own wording, like creatures, company or army, so the word takes in every kind of created thing rather than one thing after another. Each kind is a world, and the people of each generation are the world of their own time. Humankind are a world, the jinn are a world, and every other race of creation is a world of its own. One outstanding man can even be called the world of his time. This is the explanation reported by the early exegetes, and it is the meaning that most of them held, that each kind of creation counts as a world of its own.

The two names have already been explained with the opening phrase, and the passage treats repeating that explanation as needless. It draws a conclusion from the words appearing twice. On the view taken here, the opening formula is not itself one of the verses of this chapter, since otherwise one would have to ask why God described Himself with it twice in verses that sit side by side.

An objection is raised, that the verse about praise comes between the two and separates them. The answer is that some exegetes read the order as reversed in meaning, taking the sense to be: praise belongs to Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, Lord of the worlds, King of the Day of Judgment. Arabic often places a description late in wording while its meaning belongs earlier.

Two readings of this word have been transmitted, a short one and a long one, and they differ in meaning rather than in sound alone. Everybody who knows Arabic agrees that the short form comes from kingship and the long form from ownership, so the first says that God is King of the Day of Judgment and the second that He owns it.

The verdict prefers the short form, King. The reason given is that whoever holds kingship alone necessarily holds ownership alone as well, while the reverse does not follow, since an owner of something is not thereby its king. Acknowledging that kingship on that Day belongs to God exclusively also excludes every creature who claimed kingship in this world. A further argument is that the chapter has already called Him Lord of all the worlds, and nothing limits that lordship to this life, so His rule reaches the Hereafter without needing a separate word for it.

A third reading, putting the word in the accusative, is set aside, because the reciters and the scholars of the community are agreed in rejecting it.

The passage treats these two words as a single expression and does not discuss the Day on its own. What the Day contributes is a time, a known occasion on which deeds are gathered up and answered for, rather than a quality or a state. The explanation therefore falls on the second word.

Judgment here means reckoning and requital for deeds, the settling of accounts rather than a legal code. The word carries that sense in Arabic usage, and a line of poetry is quoted in which fighters say that they requite their opponents the like of what they were given. Two other verses are brought in to fix the sense. One says that people deny the Judgment while guardians are set over them recording what they do. The other asks why a dying man cannot save himself, if he is not in fact to be recompensed. The passage notes that the same word has further meanings in Arabic, which are left to be explained where they occur, so that nothing belonging elsewhere is imported into this verse.

The explanation given is: to You, O Allah, we bow in humility, abase ourselves and submit, acknowledging Your lordship and no one else's. A report from one of the companions carries the same sense, though the passage prefers to state it as humility and submission rather than as hope and fear, because worship in Arabic originally means submissiveness. The examples offered are ordinary ones. A road worn flat by traffic is described with the same root, as is a camel made docile by being ridden, and a slave is called a slave from his submissiveness to his master. Hope and fear are present in worship, but they are not what the word names.

Putting "You" before the verb has a grammatical reason. The pronoun belongs to the verb and would have been attached to its end, but when it is brought forward Arabic adds a support, since a noun cannot stand as a single letter on its own. The forward position is also what makes the sentence exclusive: You alone, and nothing else.

The order of the two halves is then questioned, since worship is only possible with help, so asking for help might seem to belong first. The answer draws a large conclusion. That God commands His servants to ask Him for help in the worship He has commanded is the clearest proof against those who hold that a person is simply left to his own power, and Muslims agree that asking God for help is right.

phrases.translation: and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help
phrases.explanation:
The meaning is: You alone, our Lord, we ask for help in worshipping You, in obeying You and in all our affairs, and no one else. The contrast drawn is with a person who turns away from God and asks help from the object he worships instead of Him.

An objection asks what sense it makes to request help with an obedience God has already commanded, and whether anyone can even say the words without already being helped, since saying them is itself an act of obedience. The answer distinguishes times. The believer is asking for help with what remains of his life and the duties still ahead of him, not with deeds already done and the part of his life already spent.

Guidance is explained here as something God does in the worshipper rather than information He hands over. The meaning preferred is: grant us the capacity to remain steadfast upon the path. One report from a companion says the same, and the capacity meant is the help that makes an action possible. In that sense the phrase amounts to the request made in the verse before it, since asking God for help and asking Him for guidance are both a servant asking to be kept upright in obedience and to hit upon the truth in what he has been told to do.

Two rival explanations are considered and set aside. The first takes the words as a request for more guidance, or for the duties to be explained. That cannot stand, because God does not oblige anyone to a duty until He has explained it and established the proof, so a person already has the explanation before he is commanded to pray at all. Any increase he asks for must concern deeds still to come, which returns the phrase to the meaning above. The second takes it as a request to be conducted along the road to the Garden in the Hereafter, comparing a verse that leads the wicked to the road of the Fire. The exegetes among the Companions and the Successors are agreed that the path in this chapter means something else, and the preceding request for help shows that what is being asked for is assistance in worship now.

So the settled reading is a request for the capacity to stay firm, in word and deed, in what pleases God, of the kind He gave to the servants He favored. The passage draws one further conclusion. A person who must ask to be kept on the path plainly does not already have everything he needs by his own power.

The exegetes are agreed that the straight path is the clear way in which there is no crookedness, and Arabic uses the word the same way, as a line of poetry is quoted to show. The word itself is connected with a road that carries the foot toward water, which is the direction a traveler cannot afford to lose.

God calls this path straight because it is the correct one, in which there is no error. A different explanation is reported, that it is called straight because it conducts its people directly to the Garden, and that is rejected on the ground that it goes against the agreement of all the exegetes, whose consensus on the opposite is itself the proof. The description belongs to the quality of the way, not to where it eventually arrives.

phrases.translation: the Path of those You have blessed
phrases.explanation:
This phrase says what the straight path is, since every way of truth is straight and the description so far has been general. The verse quoted to explain it names the people concerned: whoever obeys God and His Messenger is among those God has favored, the prophets, the truthful, the witnesses and the righteous. So the path asked for is the road of people God has already described in revelation, and He has promised that whoever walks it and stays firm, obedient to God and His Messenger, will be brought where they arrived, a promise He does not break.

Two things follow. One concerns how the favor is worded. The blessing is attached to God, who bestowed it, and not to the people who received it, which the passage takes as clear proof that obedience is reached only because God gives it and grants the capacity for it. The other is grammatical and affects the phrase that follows, since the wording is left indefinite in sense, and Arabic does not allow a definite term to be qualified by an indefinite one carrying its case ending.

Every reciter reads this word in the genitive, and the passage sets out why that is possible, because the answer changes the meaning. Two routes are given. On the first, the word qualifies "those" and follows its case, which is allowed even though "those" is definite and the qualifier indefinite, because the phrase "those You have blessed" is indefinite in sense, naming a group by a quality rather than by a known list. On the second, the genitive repeats the earlier noun, giving "the path of those You have blessed, the path of not those under wrath", so the second group is simply other people than the first. A third possibility, reading the word in the accusative, is explained and then set aside, because it departs from what the community transmitted, and a reading that departs from widespread transmission is not to be preferred. The passage is explicit about why it spends time on grammar at all: the case endings decide whether this phrase describes the first group or excludes a different one.

The verdict keeps the first reading, so the phrase qualifies those whom God has favored, and asks that they not be people under wrath.

What wrath means is then examined. Some explained it as a blameworthy reproof from God and a rebuke of the deeds. Others held that it is a real meaning of the kind we understand by wrath, while insisting that its character in God differs from anger in human beings, which disturbs and overwhelms the one who feels it, since deficiency does not inhabit Him.

A last question concerns the word "not" itself. Some took it to mean "other than", which would make the sense: the path of those You favored, other than those under wrath and those who stray. Grammarians of Kufa objected that the following "nor" cannot hang on "other than". That objection is accepted as the better view, because the word has only three meanings in Arabic, exception, negation, and "other than", and since the other two fail here, it must be a negation.

Straying is explained from the language. Anyone who turns aside from the right way and follows a method other than it is called a strayer, because he has missed the direction of the road. On that basis the passage reports how the first exegetes understood the two groups named in this verse, reading those under wrath as the Jews of the Prophet's own time and those who stray as the Christians, communities known to the earliest Muslims and described here as they stood in that history, not as a statement about people living now.

The small word "nor" is also examined. Arabic uses it in a way that sets something aside and rounds off a negation, and the passage brings poetry, together with another verse in which the same construction means the opposite of what it appears to mean, to show that the wording here simply carries the negation forward: not those under wrath, and not those who stray.

A theological objection is then answered. Some argued that because straying is attached to the people who stray, while God does not describe Himself as the one who made them stray, the verse proves that human beings act on their own. That is dismissed as ignorance of how wide Arabic is. If an attribute always had to be traced to its cause, it would be wrong to say "the tree moved" when the wind moved it, or "the earth shook" when the quake shook it. The passage is firm that God is the One who guides and who lets go astray, and that nothing else does either. The Quran was simply sent in the language of the Arabs, whose habit is to attach an action to the one from whom it proceeded, even when its cause is someone else.
